page11_img_2.png.title: Tuning time vs repository size (log–log scatter)
page11_img_2.png.description: Log-log scatter plot of tuning time (seconds, y-axis) versus repository size in number of files (x-axis), with both axes on logarithmic scales (x ≈ 10–100,000 files; y ≈ 1–1000 seconds). Blue markers show individual repositories and display a clear upward trend: larger repositories generally require more tuning time (e.g., the largest repository at ~100,000 files takes about 370 seconds). Two red markers are highlighted as outliers that take substantially longer than other repositories of similar size; the paper explains these outliers arise because those repositories have a higher average number of files changed per commit, increasing the cost of each association-rule mining run.

page7_img_1.png.title: Rex pull‑request suggestion showing recommended correlated file edits
page7_img_1.png.description: Screenshot of a Rex-generated pull-request comment that recommends additional files to edit. The top contains a short explanatory sentence telling the engineer that other files are often changed together with the files in this PR. A three-column table (partially visible) highlights the suggested file path (center column, shown as a masked /src/... path) and a right-hand cell that reports how many past PRs edited both sets of files (numeric value masked). Below the table are brief actions/feedback instructions (e.g., mark the comment as relevant or "Won't Fix") and a link for comments or questions; sensitive text has been redacted in the image.

page8_img_1.png.title: Repository characteristics (min/max values)
page8_img_1.png.description: The table reports four repository metrics with their observed minimum and maximum values across the deployed set: (1) Total number of files: 26 (min) to 99,235 (max); (2) Percentage of config files in a repository: 16% to 100%; (3) Average number of pull-requests per day: 1 to 279; (4) Number of engineers: 3 to 2,885. These min/max ranges illustrate the large heterogeneity of repositories on which Rex runs — from tiny or config-only repos to very large, highly active ones — supporting the paper’s point that models must be tuned per repository and over time.

page11_img_1.png.title: Variation of tuned s_min and normalized precision/recall/F1 for four repositories
page11_img_1.png.description: The figure shows results for four repositories (columns a–d). The top row (panels a–d) are scatter plots of the tuned minimum-support s_min values over time for each repository (time on the x-axis, tuned s_min on the y-axis), illustrating that s_min fluctuates substantially across time and repositories. The bottom row (panels e–h) plots normalized recall (blue dotted), precision (red), and F1-score (black) as functions of s_min (x-axis) for the corresponding repositories; values are normalized relative to the baseline model with s_min = 4. Across all four repositories recall declines as s_min increases, while precision responds differently per repository (e.g., precision increases with s_min predictably for Repo4 and to some extent Repo2, but is non-monotonic or decreases for Repo1 and Repo3), and the F1 curve has a clear maximum (marked) used to select the deployed s_min.

page10_img_1.png.title: Model vs Deployment Precision for Change-Rule Discovery (Table 3)
page10_img_1.png.description: Table 3 reports per-repository counts and precision for Rex’s change-rule discovery step, separately for model evaluation (on six months of held-out test data) and for live deployment. For each of seven repositories (Exchange1–3, Azure1, OneDrive1–2, DynamicsCRM1) it lists Total suggestions, True Positives, False Positives and Precision under both Model Metrics and Deployment Metrics. Model precision is substantially higher (66.09% for DynamicsCRM1 up to 82.11% for Azure1) while deployment precision is much lower and more variable (6.84% for Azure1 up to 18.52% for OneDrive2); for example Exchange1 had model precision 71.80% (1342/1869) but deployment precision 9.63% (50/519). These numbers illustrate the paper’s point that many learned correlations look correct on historical data but far fewer result in actionable suggestions in active pull-requests, producing a large gap between model and deployment precision.

page10_img_2.png.title: Change-rule refinement (CRR) improves model and deployment precision
page10_img_2.png.description: The table compares model and deployment precision, before and after applying change-rule refinement (CRR), for six repositories (Exchange1, Exchange2, Exchange3, Azure1, OneDrive2, DynamicsCRM1). For each repository it shows Precision (Without CRR), Precision (With CRR) and the percent improvement for both Model Metrics and Deployment Metrics. CRR increases model precision in every case (e.g., DynamicsCRM1: 66.09% → 89.64%, +35.64 percentage points) and produces large gains in deployment precision (notably Exchange3: 5.04% → 18.00%, a 250.42% relative increase; OneDrive2: 37.50% → 100.00%, +62.50 percentage points). These results (for XML/config file types supported by the refinement step) indicate that syntactic refinement substantially reduces false positives and makes suggestions more actionable in deployment.

page5_img_2.png.title: Example change-rules learned: file associations and suggested correlated edits
page5_img_2.png.description: Three boxed example rules learned by Rex’s change-rule discovery are shown. (a) /.../ServiceLibrary/package.xml ⇒ /.../ServiceLibrary/src/NuGetPackage/NuGetPackage.nuproj represents a rule where a change to a package XML typically requires a corresponding version-number update in the NuGet project file. (b) /.../configuration/dailyRun.xml ⇒ /.../configuration/dogfoodRun.xml captures nearly identical configuration files that tend to be edited together. (c) /.../Framework/src/Actions/RunDailyWorkflows.cs, /.../Config/Engine.Settings.ini ⇒ /.../Config/DWEngine.flight.ini illustrates a multi-file LHS rule: when code and a related settings file are added/changed, a flighting configuration file is also usually required. These examples highlight that discovered rules can involve multiple source files and cross file-type correlations (code ↔ configuration) prior to refinement.

page9_img_1.png.title: Tuned minimum support (s_min) vs repository size (scatter)
page9_img_1.png.description: A scatter plot showing, for each of the 360 repositories, the tuned minimum support s_min (y-axis) against repository size in number of files (x-axis, plotted on a logarithmic scale). Most repositories—across a wide range of sizes—cluster at low s_min values around 4–10, but there is a clear upward trend: the largest repositories require much higher s_min (the largest point near 100,000 files has s_min ≈ 40). The paper reports a moderate correlation (0.56) between repository size and s_min, yet the wide vertical spread at some sizes (e.g., around 700 files s_min ranges from ~4 to ~23) illustrates that repository-specific tuning is necessary and repository size alone does not determine the best s_min.

page6_img_1.png.title: Anti-unification of XML diffs to generalize correlated configuration changes
page6_img_1.png.description: The figure illustrates change-rule refinement: three concrete commits to a Network XML fragment (with RackTypes="Capacity", RackTypes="Managment", RackTypes="FrontEnd" and CommandConfig values "enable IPv6", "add route", "add subnet NAT") are each converted by a differencing step into difference trees that capture the syntactic additions. Those difference trees are fed to an anti-unification algorithm which produces a most-specific generalization (a regular-expression-like pattern) that replaces the varying attribute and node text with wildcards (e.g., RackTypes = * and CommandConfig = *). The resulting generalized difference tree is shown both as a tree and as a template XML snippet (<Network RackTypes=* xmlns="DeployCfg"> <CommandConfig>*</CommandConfig> </Network>), which Rex uses to refine an X ⇒ Y change-rule so suggestions are made only when a new change matches this generalized pattern.

page5_img_1.png.title: Rex architecture: client, suggestion engine, and rule‑learning engine
page5_img_1.png.description: Block diagram of Rex showing three logical components and their data flows: a Rex Client, the Rex Suggestion Engine, and the Rex Rule‑Learning Engine. The client notifies the suggestion engine when a file is changed (arrow labeled "1.File Changed"); the suggestion engine queries the rule‑learning engine (which holds commit logs and runs change‑rule discovery, change‑rule refinement, and parameter tuning) to obtain change‑rules and returns suggestions to the client ("2.Suggestion"). Engineer responses are captured as implicit feedback (arrow "3.Feedback") into a "Change‑rule feedback" artifact in the suggestion engine and routed back to the rule‑learning engine’s parameter tuning, closing the loop that updates the learned rules based on deployment behavior.

page3_img_table_1.png.title: Eight real examples of correlated file changes and their impacts
page3_img_table_1.png.description: The table enumerates eight real cases Rex flagged, with columns for File 1, File 2, the reason the files are correlated, and the consequence if File 2 is left unchanged. It lists concrete file-type pairs (e.g., source JS + test JS; C# component definitions replicated across frameworks; INI feature settings + flight definitions; XML microservice registry + firewall rules; PS1 script + XML vulnerability list; PS1 caller/callee scripts; SCSS + C# flighting; XML SKU info + rack definitions) and the practical outcomes (for example: an added feature missing its test, incorrectly suppressed alerts, the feature not deploying, a security threat from mismatched firewall entries or stale vulnerability line numbers, deployment failure from a changed script function, UI deployment delays, or data-center configuration disruption). These rows illustrate the paper’s categories (testing, replication, flighting, microservice/configuration updates, scripting, and miscellaneous high-impact corner cases) and show why missing correlated changes can range from reduced code quality to severe security or service outages. The table shows only two-file examples for clarity, though the authors note real change-rules can involve more than two files.
